opus-5.5.text:
I think it's useful, but much less useful than people tend to assume. A lot of things you learn at 7B or 14B simply don't transfer cleanly. At small scale you can run many experiments quickly, try lots of data mixtures, tweak hyperparameters, and you build a kind of intuition. That intuition is valuable for the basics: how to build a stable training pipeline, how to clean data, how to set up evaluation, how to debug when the loss curve looks strange. That engineering muscle carries over.

But many of the conclusions don't. Some data recipes that clearly help a small model barely matter for a large one, and sometimes the opposite happens. Capabilities like complex reasoning, or the model's ability to make use of certain kinds of high-quality data, only really appear once the model is big enough. So if you judge a dataset or a method purely by its effect on a 7B model, you can end up throwing away something that would have been very important at scale, or betting on something that stops mattering.

Stability is another area. Problems with large-scale training, like loss spikes, numerical issues, and communication and infrastructure bottlenecks across thousands of cards, often don't show up at all at small scale. You only meet them when you actually go big.

So my view is that small models are a good place to build the foundation and run fast ablations, but you have to stay humble about extrapolating from them. You want scaling experiments across several sizes so you can see the trend rather than trust a single point. And eventually some decisions can only be validated on the big model itself. That's also why teams that have actually trained very large models have an advantage that's hard to copy. That kind of experience is something you can't fully get from small models.

r001.rationale: The response says experience at 7B or 14B is less useful than often assumed and that many lessons and conclusions do not transfer cleanly to much larger models.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's useful, but with real limits. The experience from 7B or 14B models helps a lot in understanding the basic laws—how data quality affects things, how learning rate and batch size should be set, how to design training stability, how to check whether a dataset is working. Those methodological habits transfer directly, and you can iterate many times on a small model, which is where most of your actual understanding of training comes from.

But many things don't transfer linearly. When you go from 14B to hundreds of billions of parameters, especially with MoE architectures, new problems appear that you simply never saw at small scale—loss spikes, expert load balancing, communication bottlenecks across thousands of GPUs, numerical precision issues. Some hyperparameters that worked well at 7B become wrong at larger scale, and you can't find that out by extrapolating; you have to run the large experiment.

So my view is that small-model experience gives you intuition and a good experimental framework, and that's necessary. But it's not sufficient. The real capability of training large models comes from actually doing it at scale, making mistakes there, and building an infrastructure and team that can handle those problems. Teams that only have small-model experience tend to underestimate how much of large-model training is actually engineering rather than algorithms.

r001.rationale: The response says experience from 7B or 14B models has “real limits,” that many things do not transfer linearly, and that large-scale training introduces problems that cannot be learned by extrapolation.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful, but you have to distinguish between experience that transfers and conclusions that transfer. Training a 7B or 14B model gives you experience with the whole process: preparing data, running experiments, diagnosing instability, and evaluating results. Those skills matter when you move to larger models.

But a recipe that works well at 7B isn’t necessarily the best recipe at a much larger scale. The effects of data mixtures, hyperparameters, and architectural choices can change. And distributed training introduces engineering problems that you may barely encounter with a smaller model.

So I would treat smaller models as a way to develop intuition and test hypotheses, rather than as proof that something will work at scale. The most valuable experience is learning how to design experiments and understand why a result happened. You still need experiments at larger scales to check which conclusions hold.

r001.rationale: The response says experience with smaller models builds transferable skills and intuition, while recipes and conclusions may not hold at larger scales and must be checked there. This communicates that the experience has limited, rather than complete, transferability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful, but the experience doesn’t transfer directly. Training a 7B or 14B model helps you understand the whole process—data preparation, optimization, evaluation, and how to diagnose problems. Those skills matter at any scale.

But when you move to a much larger model, you encounter problems that may barely show up at the smaller scale: training stability, communication overhead, hardware failures, and coordinating a much larger system. A method that works well on 7B also won’t necessarily give you the same improvement on a larger model.

So I’d treat small-model training as a foundation and a way to test ideas, but you still need to validate those ideas as you scale. It’s valuable experience; it just isn’t a substitute for actually training large models.

r001.rationale: The response says experience with 7B or 14B models is useful but does not transfer directly, and that methods must be validated when scaling to much larger models.
